title: Refactoring without destroying
summary: Rename with moved blocks, stop managing with removed blocks, adopt existing objects with import blocks, and the terraform state commands they replace.

steps.title: A rename is a destroy, unless you say otherwise
body: Rename `random_pet.server` to `random_pet.web` in the code and Terraform sees one address disappear and a new one
appear: **destroy the old, create a new**. For a database that is a disaster. Tell Terraform it is the same object:
```hcl
moved {
from = random_pet.server
to   = random_pet.web
The plan then says `# random_pet.server has moved to random_pet.web` and changes nothing. A `moved` block is code: it
is reviewed in the pull request, works in every environment and workspace when they next apply, and can stay in the
code (modules that others use should keep them for a while). It also works for moving into a module
(`to = module.web.random_pet.this`) and from `count` to `for_each` (`from = x[0]`, `to = x["a"]`).
The old way is `terraform state mv random_pet.server random_pet.web`: it edits the state directly, at once, in one
environment, with no review. It still has its uses (one-off fixes, moving between two states), but prefer `moved`.

steps.title: Rename to the naming standard
prompt: The team's naming standard says resources are named after their role. In `~/infra/shop`, rename:
Nothing may be destroyed or created: the server keeps its name. Plan first, read it, then apply.

checks.name: the state has the new addresses
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/shop && terraform state list | grep -qx random_pet.web && terraform state list | grep -qx local_file.web_nginx && ! terraform state list | grep -qxE 'random_pet.server|local_file.nginx'
checks.fail: `terraform state list` should show `random_pet.web` and `local_file.web_nginx`, and not the old names. Did you apply?

checks.name: the server kept its name
checks.fail: The server's name changed, so `random_pet` was destroyed and created again. Press Reset scenario and use `moved` blocks.

hints: Rename both blocks (and the references to `random_pet.server`), then add one `moved` block per rename.
`grep -n 'random_pet.server\|local_file." *"nginx' main.tf` finds every place to change. The plan must say *has moved to*, never *will be destroyed*.

`sed -i 's/random_pet" "server"/random_pet" "web"/; s/random_pet.server/random_pet.web/g; s/local_file" "nginx"/local_file" "web_nginx"/' main.tf`, then a `moved.tf` with two `moved { from = ... to = ... }` blocks.
steps.explain: Plan: `0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy` with two *has moved to* notes. The apply only rewrote addresses in the state. Leave the `moved` blocks in until every environment has applied them; removing one too early turns the rename back into a destroy for whoever is behind.

steps.title: Stop managing it, without deleting it
body: Sometimes an object should leave this configuration but keep existing: another team takes it over, or it moves to a
different state. Deleting the block would **destroy** it. Since Terraform 1.7, say so in code instead:
```hcl
removed {
from = tls_private_key.api
lifecycle {
destroy = false
The plan says `will no longer be managed by Terraform, but will not be destroyed`; after the apply, the address is
gone from the state and the real object is untouched. The other team then adopts it with an `import` block. The old
way is `terraform state rm ADDRESS`, again direct and unreviewed.

steps.title: Hand robots.txt to the SEO team
prompt: The SEO team now manages `robots.txt` from their own configuration. Make `~/infra/shop` stop managing
`local_file.robots`, **without deleting the file**: their import will pick it up from where it is.
Remove its `resource` block, add the right `removed` block, plan (read the warning), and apply.

checks.name: robots is no longer in this state
checks.fail: `terraform state list` still shows `local_file.robots`. Apply a plan with a `removed` block.

checks.name: the file was not deleted
checks.fail: `out/robots.txt` is gone: it was destroyed. Press Reset scenario and use `removed` with `lifecycle { destroy = false }`.

checks.name: the code says so
checks.fail: The `resource "local_file" "robots"` block should be gone, a `removed` block with `destroy = false` in its place, and `terraform plan` clean.

hints: Add `removed { from = local_file.robots` with `lifecycle { destroy = false } }` in a new file, for example `removed.tf`.
`terraform plan -out=tfplan` must say *will no longer be managed by Terraform, but will not be destroyed*. Then `terraform apply tfplan`.
steps.explain: Deleting the block alone would have planned `- local_file.robots ... will be destroyed (because local_file.robots is not in configuration)` and removed the file. With a cloud object the stakes are higher: the real thing keeps running and the other team imports it by its ID. `destroy = false` is the safe form to remember; a `removed` block without it is how you delete something on purpose, with a reviewable diff.

steps.title: Adopt what already exists: import blocks
body: Things built by hand (or by another tool) can be brought under Terraform without rebuilding them. Write where it
should go and the provider's **import ID** for it:
```hcl
import {
to = aws_s3_bucket.logs
id = "shop-prod-logs-example"        # the ID format is on each resource's registry page
`terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf` writes a `resource` block from what the provider reads. Review it,
tidy it into your files, and plan until it says `1 to import, 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy`: if the block
does not match the real object, the plan shows the changes (or a replacement) the import would cause. Import blocks
work in modules (Terraform 1.16+), with `for_each`, and in every environment; `terraform import ADDR ID` is the old
one-shot command.

steps.title: Adopt the reporting admin password
prompt: The reporting database's admin password was set by hand in 2024 (`~/legacy/wiki-page.txt`). Bring it under
Terraform as `random_password.reporting_admin` **without changing it** (the import ID of a `random_password` is the
password itself). Let Terraform generate the block, check that the plan imports and changes nothing else, and apply.
Afterwards delete the wiki copy of the password: the state is now the single place it lives.

checks.name: the password is imported unchanged
checks.fail: `random_password.reporting_admin` should be in the state with the original value. Use an `import` block and apply.

checks.name: plan is clean
checks.fail: `terraform plan` should show no changes: the resource block must match what was imported (length and character sets).

checks.name: the wiki copy is gone
checks.fail: Delete `~/legacy/wiki-page.txt` once the password is in Terraform.

hints: `terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf` writes the resource block. Read it: `length = 20`. Then plan again: `1 to import, 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy`.
steps.explain: The generated block has `length = 20`, the length of the real password; a block with a different length would have planned a **replacement** right after the import, generating a new password. That check ("does the plan after import change anything?") is the whole art of importing. Once applied, the `import` block can be deleted or left as a record; it does nothing more. For real secrets, mind lesson 1: the value is now in the state.

steps.prompt: Match the job to the block (or command).
pairs: rename a resource without destroying it
stop managing an object but keep it
adopt an object built by hand
write a resource block for an import

steps.prompt: You move three resources into a new module `module.cdn` and add `moved` blocks. Staging applied it last week; production has not. A teammate deletes the `moved` blocks as "cleanup". What happens at the next production apply?
options: Production plans to destroy the three old addresses and create three new ones
Nothing: staging already recorded the moves
Terraform remembers the moves in the lock file
The plan fails with a cycle error
steps.explain: Each state records only its own history. Production's state still has the old addresses; without the `moved` blocks it sees one set disappear and another appear. Keep `moved` blocks until every state that uses the code has applied them (for a shared module: a major version or longer).
